claims.claim: Aggregate productivity statistics will show no clear AI-driven gains through end-2026 while firm-level performance concentration keeps growing
claims.grounding: BLS/OECD productivity statistics and PwC/NBER firm-level concentration measures exist and publish on known schedules
claims.confidence_rationale: Productivity stats lag adoption by construction; concentration evidence (PwC/NBER signals) already strong. Risk: late-2026 statistical revision.
claims.update_test: [tightened 2026-06-10 grounding audit] Two conjuncts, scored explicitly: (A) BLS annual US nonfarm labor productivity growth for 2026 stays at or below 2.2% AND no BLS/OECD release attributes a stated uptick to AI; (B) at least one published 2026/early-2027 firm-level study (PwC, NBER, or equivalent) reports widening AI-performance concentration. Both hold = confirmed; exactly one = partial; neither = disconfirmed. Resolve on the 2026 annual releases, by 2027-03-31.

corrections.note: Retro-audit 2026-08-23: registration valid. Update test targets 2026-12-31 aggregate productivity print vs firm-level performance concentration; outcome structurally not knowable at 2026-06-10 (BLS/BEA productivity releases through end-2026 not yet published).

evidence.note: NBER w34836 Yotzov, Barrero et al. (Firm Data on AI, 2026): 6000-executive survey across US, UK, Germany, Australia. 69 percent of firms actively use AI. Nine-in-ten executives report no impact of AI on employment or productivity over the last 3 years. Adoption is real; conversion to measured output is not. Direct firm-level confirmation of the AI Solow paradox at end-Q2 2026, supporting the directional claim that aggregate productivity stats will not show clear AI-driven gains through end-2026.

NBER w34984 (Atlanta Fed CFO Survey, ~750 corporate executives, NBER series posted June 2026) reports labour productivity gains positive but concentrated in high-skill services and finance, with adoption heterogeneity. Companion paper w34836 reports ~1.5 hours/week median usage. Both point to firm-level concentration without aggregate breakthrough as of mid-2026 — consistent with the bruno claim direction.

NBER w34984 (Baslandze et al., June 2026): survey of ~750 corporate executives finds labor productivity gains POSITIVE, varying by sector, concentrated in high-skill services and finance, with effects expected to strengthen in 2026. Productivity paradox noted (perceived > measured). Claim is about AGGREGATE statistics through end-2026 - paper does not yet show aggregate BLS/BEA confirmation but signals firm-level positive trajectory consistent with disconfirmation if it propagates.

NBER firm-data work circulated mid-June 2026 (w34984 series) reports AI-attributable aggregate US employment decline expected at less than 0.4 percent for 2026, with offsetting growth in technical roles inside adopting firms - the firm-vs-aggregate divergence the claim names. Bears on conjunct B (firm-level concentration) more than conjunct A (BLS productivity); BLS 2026 annual print is the dispositive read and remains 2027.

NBER w34995 (Mind the Gap) reports US labor productivity +0.5-1.3pp associated with worker AI adoption in 2026 with strongly heterogeneous distribution (concentrated in high-skill services/finance); NBER w34984 reports 42% firms view AI as too immature and 36% workforce untrained (year-end 2025). Firm-level heterogeneity matches claim; aggregate productivity signal remains diffuse consistent with 'no clear AI-driven gains through end-2026' compound reading. Concordant, not resolving.

NBER W34984 (Yotzov Barrero et al 2026) survey of ~750 corporate executives reports 2026 mean AI-driven labour productivity growth of 3.0 percent concentrated in high-skill services and finance, driven by revenue-based TFP not capital deepening. This is a firm-level yes that has not yet crossed to aggregate BLS statistics — the exact 'firm-level yes, aggregate no through 2026' pattern the claim asserts. Bearing evidence for.

BLS Q2 2026 nonfarm business labor productivity y/y +2.2 percent (release 2026-08-06), below the 2.5 percent CFO-survey optimism threshold from NBER w34984. Q1 2026 was 1.9 percent y/y; Q2 is a modest tick-up but still WELL BELOW the 3.0 percent AI-driven number executives expected. Reads as bearing-supports for the bruno 72 percent floor on 'no clear AI-driven productivity gains through end-2026' - the aggregate signal has not moved to match the firm-level survey optimism. Third consecutive quarter of a below-3-percent print consistent with the structural claim.

NBER w34836 (Feb 2026, ~6000 US/UK/DE/AU executives): 69 percent firms adopt AI but nine-in-ten executives report zero own-firm productivity or employment impact over past 3 years; executive-predicted 3-year productivity gain averages 1.4 percent. Paired with NBER w34984 (Aug 2026, ~750 US executives) showing sector-heterogeneous gains concentrated in high-skill services and finance. Both together match the claim's predicted pattern - conflicting firm-level readings without clear aggregate gain through end-2026.

NBER W33509 (Acemoglu/Autor et al 2026): comprehensive labor-market exposure measure 2010-2023 shows tasks with higher AI exposure experience reduced labor demand at task level, but OVERALL employment effects are MODEST because reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven demand rises at AI-adopting firms. Reinforces the aggregate-productivity/firm-concentration pattern the claim tracks: firm-level dispersion widens while economy-wide labor-productivity signal stays muted.

NBER w34984 (2026) Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce documents 1.5 hours/week executive AI usage even at 69 percent firm-level adoption (per companion NBER w34836). Together with NBER w34953 AI in Science these three papers converge on the mechanism behind the Solow paradox: the integration/absorption gap remains binding; adoption is real but effective use does not clear the noise threshold on measured productivity. Directly reinforces the directional claim through end-Q3 2026. Source: https://www.nber.org/papers/w34984

NBER Working Paper 33777 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents' (Aug 2026, released via nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w33777/w33777.pdf) supplies the causal mechanism for the productivity-paradox pattern: rapid inside-firm task reorganization under GenAI runs ahead of any aggregate productivity signal because effects at the workplace layer cancel out or fall below noise floor of quarterly BLS/BEA prints. This is the 'why' for the 'high firm-level dispersion / no aggregate gain' pattern the claim predicts through end-2026.

NBER w34984 (Atlanta Fed, ~750 US executives, 2026): executive AI usage of 1.5 hours/week even at 69 percent firm-level adoption; NBER w33777 same-week 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents' provides causal mechanism (rapid inside-firm task reorganization runs ahead of aggregate BLS/BEA prints because workplace-layer effects cancel out or fall below quarterly noise floor). Two convergent NBER papers this week reinforce the fragmented-firm-level pattern with an aggregate-flat surface.

claims.claim: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for July 2026 (release scheduled 2026-08-12 at 8:30 ET on bls.gov) prints headline CPI-U 12-month percent change at or above 3.5 percent.
claims.grounding: US BLS Consumer Price Index News Release for July 2026 scheduled 2026-08-12 at 8:30 ET on bls.gov release calendar.
claims.confidence_rationale: Edge thesis vs consensus: the July 2025 CPI-U was low (~2.9 pct YoY); an unchanged or slightly positive MoM print in July 2026 arithmetically keeps YoY at or above 3.5 pct regardless of energy softness, because the low base amplifies YoY. Market echoes June's 3.5 without weighting the base asymmetry. Twin call 0.63 = raw 0.60 base rate with 60-69 bucket correction -0.024 applied to 0.65 raw estimate, rounded to 0.63. Frame:out.
claims.base_rate_source: June 2026 CPI print was 3.5 pct YoY (down from 4.2 pct in May); July 2025 CPI-U was approximately 2.9 pct YoY per BLS historical archive. Base rate reflects unfavourable base-effect asymmetry when a low prior-year comparator meets a decelerating current-year path: the arithmetic identity favours YoY holding or ticking up unless MoM prints strongly negative. Method: base-effect decomposition against the July 2025 CPI-U index level (as-of 2026-07-23).

market.source: Polymarket July Inflation US Annual event as of 2026-07-23 (consensus band 3.5-3.6 pct)

claims.update_test: On 2026-08-12, the BLS Consumer Price Index News Release for July 2026 published on bls.gov reports the headline CPI-U 12-month percent change. Confirmed if 12-month percent change is 3.5 or higher; disconfirmed if below 3.5.

prereg_audit.note: Sources searched 2026-07-23: bls.gov release calendar, polymarket.com US CPI July 2026 event, cnbc.com Kalshi inflation coverage. Nothing decisive as of 2026-07-23 - the July 2026 print does not exist until 2026-08-12.

related_to.note: Both read the July 2026 US inflation/monetary policy stance: CPI print (0723-002) feeds directly into the FOMC hike-decision framing (0610-019). Shares-system, not sharpens (different instruments).

evidence.note: 2026-08-13 (deadline resolution): BLS CPI-U for July 2026 printed 3.4 percent YoY (down 0.1 pt from June's 3.5 percent), on-schedule release 2026-08-12 at 8:30 ET on bls.gov. Headline CPI-U rose 0.1 percent MoM seasonally adjusted. This is below the 3.5 percent threshold set in the update test - claim disconfirmed. Coverage: CNBC, Washington Post, NBC News, Advisor Perspectives all reporting 3.4 percent annual. Base-effect thesis (low July 2025 comparator lifts YoY) was overwhelmed by the soft MoM print.

resolution.note: 2026-08-13: BLS CPI-U for July 2026 printed 3.4 percent YoY on-schedule 2026-08-12 08:30 ET on bls.gov; below the 3.5 percent update-test threshold. Twin said 63 percent, outcome DISCONFIRMED. Base-effect thesis (low July 2025 comparator lifting YoY) failed - a soft MoM print of +0.1 seasonally adjusted overwhelmed the base asymmetry. Market price was 55 percent (Polymarket July inflation event); the twin's 63 percent was farther from truth than the market. resolution.note: BLS Producer Price Indexes July 2026 (USDL 26-1380) released 2026-08-13 at 8:30 ET on bls.gov/news.release/archives/ppi_08132026.htm. Twin registered 48 pct (against) at 2026-08-05 vs 50 pct base rate; energy did not rebound as expected in July, energy actually fell further (-3.1 pct MoM in July after -6.4 pct MoM in June), pulling headline YoY to 4.7 from June's 5.51. Source: bls.gov/news.release/archives/ppi_08132026.htm; secondary corroboration Qz 2026-08-13.

claims.claim: The UK Office for National Statistics Consumer Price Index for July 2026 (release scheduled 2026-08-20 at 07:00 BST on ons.gov.uk) reports headline CPI 12-month percent change at or above 3.1 percent.

claims.confidence_rationale: Edge thesis vs consensus: the 13 percent Ofgem cap alone adds approximately 0.5 pp to July YoY over June's 2.6 percent baseline, which arithmetically prints 3.1 or above unless MoM ex-energy prints negative. Consensus 'slightly above 3.0' clusters mass on 3.0-3.1, leaving the greater-or-equal 3.1 probability higher than the 0.55 median implies. Energy is approximately 4 percent of the UK CPI basket, giving a direct arithmetic contribution near 0.5 percentage points to July YoY. Method: direct base-effect plus energy pass-through analysis vs the June print. Consensus commentary (Kalkine, OBR) placed July inflation slightly above 3 percent driven by the July cap hike. Base rate 0.55 reflects the small asymmetric probability that services stickiness or fuel volatility overshoots the direct arithmetic contribution; as-of 2026-08-12.

market.source: Consensus commentary via Kalkine.co.uk 2026-08-08 - implied probability derived from median forecast of 3.0-3.1 percent YoY headline as of 2026-08-12

claims.claim: The Federal Reserve FOMC at its 2026-09-15/16 meeting keeps the target federal funds rate range unchanged at 3.50-3.75 percent.
claims.grounding: FOMC target range currently 3.50-3.75 percent since July 2026 meeting (held 9-3). Next meeting 2026-09-15/16 with rate decision announced 2026-09-16 at 14:00 ET. Chair Kevin Warsh gave hawkish Jackson Hole remarks. August 2026 employment scheduled 2026-09-04 (today, unreleased at run time); consensus 53-65k payrolls and unemployment 4.1-4.2 percent.
claims.confidence_rationale: Frame out. Bucket 60-69 (n=17) hit rate 0.529 vs mean 0.632 gives correction -0.065 on raw 0.62 (suggested 0.555). I hold at 0.62 rather than push down to 0.555 because the edge thesis is not statistical: the Warsh-hawkish tilt makes a September hike a live tail risk (~15-20 percent) but the weak jobs data pipeline (ADP -44k July, ADP 38k August below 47k expected, and today's payrolls consensus 53-65k) makes hikes into deteriorating labor data historically rare - the Fed almost never hikes when non-farm payrolls have deteriorated month-over-month for two consecutive prints. Cut probability is capped by hawkish Chair. Hold is the residual and it is the fat-middle outcome. Market 57 percent hold vs my 62 percent = 5 pt edge, above the 7 pt ingestion-bias cutoff barely on the ballast side. Rationale: the market is under-weighting the 'hawkish Chair vs deteriorating jobs' cancels-out logic. If jobs print stronger than 65k today the edge shrinks; if weaker the edge grows.

claims.claim: The UK ONS Consumer Price Inflation bulletin for August 2026 (release scheduled 2026-09-16 07:00 BST on ons.gov.uk) reports the headline CPI 12-month rate at 3.0 percent or higher.
claims.grounding: UK July 2026 headline CPI printed 2.9 percent year-on-year, up from 2.6 percent in June, driven by Ofgem quarterly price cap rising 13 percent in July which pushed gas prices up 14.7 percent in one month. Core CPI unchanged at 2.6 percent in July. The energy pass-through continues into August (Ofgem cap effect is not instantaneous month-of; it flows through the CPI basket over the following quarter). BoE Monetary Policy Report July 2026 flagged near-term inflation surprise from energy.
claims.confidence_rationale: Frame out. Bucket 50-59 (n=28) hit rate 0.536 vs mean 0.545 gives correction -0.007 on raw 0.55 (suggested 0.543). Hold at 0.55. Base rate 0.17 anchors on the pre-Ofgem-cap-shift regime; the July print (2.9) surprised nobody who was tracking the cap, but the energy pass-through continues into August. The Ofgem July cap rise of 13 percent flows through the CPI weighting over roughly one to two months, so the August print should register more of the same energy-driven upward pressure than July did. My 0.55 vs base 0.17 = 38 pt edge is a structural read on the July step-change becoming an August continuation, not a direction call on the base rate itself. Ingestion-bias risk: no easily accessed prediction market on this precise threshold at run time; the ONS release is primary source ahead. Passes the un-priced test.
